claims.claim: The Congressional Record is the official record of the proceedings and debates of the United States Congress.
claims.sourceSpan: The Congressional Record is the official record of the proceedings and debates of the United States Congress.

claims.claim: It is published on every day Congress is in session.
claims.sourceSpan: It is published daily when Congress is in session.

claims.claim: Material can be printed in the Record without ever being spoken or read on the floor.
claims.sourceSpan: Senators and Representatives may have remarks and other extraneous material, not necessarily pertaining to legislation, printed in the Record without ever speaking or reading the text on the floor.

claims.claim: Extensions of Remarks is where the bulk of that undelivered House material appears.
claims.sourceSpan: contains the bulk of House undelivered remarks and other insertions

claims.claim: The Record is published by the Government Publishing Office.
claims.sourceSpan: Government Publishing Office

claims.claim: The Record carries the debate on bills and resolutions.
claims.sourceSpan: Debate on bills and resolutions usually follows.

claims.claim: The Record shows the rollcall and voice votes taken on measures.
claims.sourceSpan: Rollcall or voice votes on amendments, passage, or tabling of measures are shown in the Record

claims.claim: It began publication in 1873.
claims.sourceSpan: The Congressional Record began publication in 1873, and is still published today.

claims.claim: GovInfo's daily Congressional Record collection covers volume 140 (1994) to the present.
claims.sourceSpan: GovInfo currently contains Congressional Record volumes from 140 (1994) to the present

claims.claim: The current year’s database is usually updated daily by 11 a.m.
claims.sourceSpan: The current year's Congressional Record database is usually updated daily by 11 a.m.

claims.claim: The Bound Congressional Record and the Record Index are separate collections on GovInfo.
claims.sourceSpan: The Bound Congressional Record and the Congressional Record Index are available as separate collections on GovInfo

claims.claim: Except for copyrighted articles, there are no restrictions on republishing material from the Record.
claims.sourceSpan: With the exception of copyrighted articles, there are no restrictions on the republication of material from the Congressional Record.

claims.claim: The Record has four main sections.
claims.sourceSpan: It consists of four main sections: the proceedings of the House and Senate, the Extensions of Remarks, and the Daily Digest.

claims.claim: The House section carries the public proceedings and debates of the House, including both words spoken on the floor and words inserted or appended by members.
claims.sourceSpan: It includes both words spoken on the floor of the House and words inserted or appended by Members of Congress.

claims.claim: House pages carry an H prefix in the format H1234.
claims.sourceSpan: Each House page begins with the letter H and appears in the format H1234.

claims.claim: The Senate section carries the public proceedings and debates of the Senate on the same terms, spoken and inserted words together.
claims.sourceSpan: It includes both words spoken and the floor of the Senate and words inserted or appended by Senators.

claims.claim: Senate pages carry an S prefix.
claims.sourceSpan: Each Senate page begins with the letter S and appears in the format S1234.

claims.claim: Statements are formatted with a speaker identifier in capitals followed by the member’s words.
claims.sourceSpan: Mr. THUNE.

claims.claim: That all-caps speaker format is what the extractor matches on.
claims.sourceSpan: // CR format: "Mr. LASTNAME." or "Mr. LASTNAME of State." (all-caps last name is distinctive).

claims.claim: Extensions of Remarks carries tributes, statements and other information supplementing floor statements from either chamber.
claims.sourceSpan: This section of the Congressional Record contains tributes, statements, and other information that supplements statements made by Members on the floor of the House or Senate.

claims.claim: Extensions of Remarks contains the bulk of House remarks that were never delivered.
claims.sourceSpan: contains the bulk of House undelivered remarks and other insertions, such as constituent tributes.

claims.claim: Extensions pages carry an E prefix (E1234).
claims.sourceSpan: Each Extensions page begins with the letter E and appears in the format E1234.

claims.claim: The Daily Digest is a table of contents for the day, opening with highlights and then a summary for each chamber.
claims.sourceSpan: The Daily Digest begins with highlights of the day

claims.claim: Each chamber summary in the Daily Digest covers measures introduced, reported, passed, or under consideration.
claims.sourceSpan: Each summary includes such items as measures introduced, reported or passed, as well measures under consideration.

claims.claim: The Daily Digest also lists committee meetings held that day and scheduled for the following day.
claims.sourceSpan: The Daily Digest also includes a list of Committee meetings held that day and scheduled for the following day

claims.claim: The daily Record's sections are numbered separately and consecutively in each session, so the page prefix identifies the section.
claims.sourceSpan: The daily Record sections are numbered separately and consecutively in each session of Congress.

claims.claim: Daily Digest pages carry a D prefix.
claims.sourceSpan: Each Digest page begins with the letter D and appears in the format D1234.

claims.claim: CRS describes the Record as a substantially verbatim account subject only to technical, grammatical, and typographical corrections.
claims.sourceSpan: The Congressional Record is a substantially verbatim account of remarks made during the proceedings of the House and Senate, subject only to technical, grammatical, and typographical corrections.
claims.section: Revise and Extend, and What It Actually Means

claims.claim: In the House a member may ask the presiding officer for permission to revise and extend.
claims.sourceSpan: Members may also revise their remarks by asking permission of the presiding officer to
claims.section: Revise and Extend, and What It Actually Means

claims.claim: CRS glosses revise and extend as expanding a statement, not retracting it.
claims.sourceSpan: expand their statements.
claims.section: Revise and Extend, and What It Actually Means

claims.claim: Members may have remarks printed in the Record without ever speaking them on the floor.
claims.sourceSpan: printed in the Record without ever speaking or reading the text on the floor.
claims.section: Revise and Extend, and What It Actually Means

claims.claim: In the Senate a bullet symbol precedes and distinguishes undelivered remarks.
claims.sourceSpan: In the Senate, a bullet symbol (!) precedes and distinguishes undelivered remarks.
claims.section: Revise and Extend, and What It Actually Means

claims.claim: In the House proceedings any portion of a statement not spoken is printed in a different type style.
claims.sourceSpan: In the House proceedings, any portion of a statement not spoken is printed in different type style.
claims.section: Revise and Extend, and What It Actually Means

claims.claim: In the Senate, with unanimous consent, undelivered remarks are printed as if spoken — so undelivered material is not always marked.
claims.sourceSpan: In the Senate, with unanimous consent, undelivered remarks are printed as if spoken.
claims.section: Revise and Extend, and What It Actually Means

claims.claim: GovInfo supports a keyword search over the full text.
claims.sourceSpan: Using basic search for keyword and metadata fielded searches

claims.claim: GovInfo results can be refined by the Record’s own metadata.
claims.sourceSpan: the sections under Refine Your Search correspond to the metadata available for the documents

claims.claim: A single document can be retrieved by citation given the volume (year), page type and page number.
claims.sourceSpan: Using the citation search to retrieve a single Congressional Record document in PDF format if you know the Volume (year), page type (House, Daily Digest, etc.), and Page Number of the document

claims.claim: CRS calls the Daily Digest the key to using the daily Record.
claims.sourceSpan: The Daily Digest is the key to use of the daily Record

claims.claim: Reading the Digest first locates the times of meetings of both houses, the measures reported, considered or signed into law, and the committee activity for the previous and current days.
claims.sourceSpan: a reader can locate the times of meetings of both houses; measures reported, considered, or signed into law

claims.claim: The Daily Digest is the last section of each daily issue and serves as an index.
claims.sourceSpan: It is the last section in each edition of the daily Record and serves as an index.

claims.claim: GovInfo breaks the Record into granules, each with its own identifier and a predictable details URL.
claims.sourceSpan: Details Page for an Individual Document Structure: https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/ {packageId}/{granuleId}

claims.claim: When a statute becomes the subject of a dispute in court, judges usually must interpret the law, ambiguous or not.
claims.sourceSpan: judges usually must interpret the law, ambiguous or not
claims.section: Why the Congressional Record Matters for Understanding Legislation

claims.claim: Legislative history is the record of Congress's deliberations when enacting a law, and is one of the tools judges may use.
claims.sourceSpan: deliberations when enacting a law.
claims.section: Why the Congressional Record Matters for Understanding Legislation

claims.claim: CRS reports that committee reports are stronger evidence of congressional understanding than individual floor statements from non-sponsors.
claims.sourceSpan: than individual floor statements from non-sponsors, for example.
claims.section: Why the Congressional Record Matters for Understanding Legislation

claims.claim: Floor statements, especially by a bill’s sponsors before passage, may be relevant but should be used cautiously.
claims.sourceSpan: but should be used cautiously.
claims.section: Why the Congressional Record Matters for Understanding Legislation

claims.claim: In one case CRS cites, the Supreme Court held that even from a sponsor a single outlying statement cannot stand against a tide of context and history.
claims.sourceSpan: a single outlying statement cannot stand against a tide of context and history
